ourAnswer: H2SO4 is an oxidising agent: it liberates HI from KI but then oxidises that HI to I2, so the alcohol is not converted to the iodide. Use the non-oxidising H3PO4 instead.
keyAnswer: H2SO4 cannot be used along with KI in the conversion of an alcohol to an alkyl iodide as it converts KI to corresponding acid, HI which is then oxidised by it to I2.
note: Same mechanism, same conclusion. Ours adds the two balanced equations and the H3PO4 remedy, which the key does not print.

keyAnswer: (i) Chloromethane, Bromomethane, Dibromomethane, Bromoform — boiling point increases with increase in molecular mass; (ii) Isopropylchloride, 1-Chloropropane, 1-Chlorobutane — isopropylchloride being branched has lower b.p. than 1-chloropropane
note: Both orders identical, and the two reasons the key gives (molecular mass; branching lowers b.p.) are the two we used.

keyAnswer: (i) CH3CH2CH2CH2Br — being primary halide, there won't be any steric hindrance; (ii) CH3CH2CH(Br)CH3 — secondary halide reacts faster than tertiary halide; (iii) CH3CH(CH3)CH2CH2Br — the presence of a methyl group closer to the halide group will increase the steric hindrance and decrease the rate
note: Same three choices. Part (iii) is the one worth noting: both compounds are primary, and the key's reason — a branch nearer the halogen slows the reaction — is exactly the argument we gave for preferring the isomer branched at C-3 over the one branched at C-2.

keyAnswer: (i) tert-butyl chloride — tertiary halide reacts faster than secondary halide because of the greater stability of the tert-carbocation; (ii) the chain bearing Cl on the second carbon — because of greater stability of secondary carbocation than primary
note: Both match. The key draws its answers as skeletal structures; its (ii) is the 2-chloro isomer, i.e. the seven-carbon chain, confirming the carbon counts we read off the PDF vector paths at transcription time.
